1296.title: Redeeming the firstborn
1296.hook: a ceremony at thirty days for a firstborn son
1296.howItsDone: When a mother's firstborn child is a son, many observant Jewish families hold a pidyon haben once he is a month old: the father gives a kohen five silver coins, blessings are said, and a festive meal follows.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was simchat bat, and your line was welcome her. Today, a ceremony with a question in the middle of it.

A father stands at a table, holding his month-old son. Across from him stands a kohen, a man from the priestly families. Between them, five silver coins. The kohen asks a strange question, from a set script handed down for the ceremony: which would you rather have, your firstborn son, or the five coins the Torah says you owe for him? The father, of course, chooses his son. He hands over the coins. The kohen takes them and blesses the child. Then everyone eats.
screen: `A FATHER, A KOHEN, FIVE COINS.` → `YOUR SON, OR THE SILVER?` → `HE CHOOSES HIS SON.`

segments.voice: Pidyon haben. Redemption of the son. First, the command. Exodus tells Israel to set apart every firstborn to God, and then says the firstborn sons are to be redeemed. Numbers gives the terms: from a month old, the redemption price is five shekels of silver, paid to the priests. So the ceremony waits until the baby has lived a month. Second, the reason. Exodus ties it to the night of the Exodus, when the firstborn of Egypt died and the firstborn of Israel were spared. When your son asks what this means, the text says, you tell him: by strength of hand God brought us out. A firstborn son is a living reminder of a night when firstborns were saved. Third, the replacement. In Numbers, God takes the Levites in place of the firstborn, to serve at the sanctuary. The firstborn are released into ordinary life, and the silver marks the release. Not every family holds the ceremony: it's for a mother's firstborn when it's a son, and families of kohanim and Levites are exempt. Fourth, the blessing. When the coins change hands, the kohen often blesses the child with the priestly blessing from Numbers: "The LORD bless thee, and keep thee." The question was never really about money. It's a way of saying, out loud, in front of witnesses: this child is a gift, and we know it.

segments.voice: Bring the scene back: the table, the coins, the question, your son or the silver? Turn it toward your own life and name one person you would never trade for anything, however the question is put, and hold their face for a few breaths. Notice when you last told them, and if you pray, give thanks for them by name.
Pidyon haben. Redemption of the firstborn son: a month old, five silver coins, a kohen's question and a blessing. Today's word.
Your line: redemption. Five coins, handed over for something no coin could buy. Rest well.

1297.title: The first haircut
1297.hook: at three, in many Hasidic and some Sephardi families
1297.howItsDone: In many Hasidic families, and in some Sephardi families with their own versions, a boy's hair is left uncut until he turns three; at the upsherin, guests each cut a lock, the side locks are left, and he often begins wearing a kippah and tzitzit.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was pidyon haben, and your line was redemption: five coins, and a father who chose his son. Today, a child turns three.

A little boy sits on his father's lap, curls down past his shoulders. He has never had a haircut. The living room is full of relatives and neighbors, and a pair of scissors is going around the room like a microphone at a wedding. One by one, each guest snips a single lock: an uncle, a grandmother, the rabbi, a cousin barely taller than the boy. Somebody's handing out candy. By the end he looks like a different child, and at the sides of his head, two locks have been left long, on purpose.
screen: `CURLS NEVER CUT.` → `THE SCISSORS GO AROUND.` → `TWO LOCKS LEFT LONG.`

segments.voice: Upsherin. A Yiddish name for a child's first haircut, held at three in many Hasidic families and, in their own versions, in some Sephardi families too. First, the tree. Leviticus says that when Israel plants a fruit tree, its fruit is not to be eaten for three years. In the fourth year it is holy, and after that it is food. And the Deuteronomy verse about fruit trees in a siege is read by some as comparing a person to a tree of the field. Some families draw the line between the two: a child, like a young tree, is left untouched for three years, and then the first harvest. It's a custom, not a written law. Second, the side locks. Leviticus also says not to round off the corners of the head. So at the first haircut, the hair at the temples is left long. These are the peyot, the side locks, and for the boy they start on this day. Third, the first things. In some families, an upsherin is also the day a boy first wears a kippah and the fringed garment called tzitzit, and some bring him to start learning his letters that week. The haircut is the outward sign; the inner change is that the child now begins to be taught. Fourth, the whole room. The custom doesn't give the scissors to a barber alone. Each guest takes a turn, and everyone who snips a curl has a hand in raising this child.

1298.title: Honey on the letters
1298.hook: a medieval custom: children licked honey from letters on their first day of learning
1298.howItsDone: Some Jewish schools and families mark a child's first Hebrew lesson by putting honey on letters for the child to taste, echoing an old custom for the first day of Torah study.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was upsherin, and your line was three years: the scissors going around, and a child who now begins to be taught. Today, the first lesson itself.

A small slate, with the Hebrew alphabet written across it: alef, bet, gimel, all the way through. Someone has spread honey over every letter. A boy, small enough that he was carried in, sits in front of it beside his teacher. The teacher points to the first letter and says its name, and the boy repeats it. Then the teacher tells him to lick the honey off. He does. Next letter, next lick. His face is sticky, he's grinning, and the grown-ups in the doorway are grinning too. That's how the custom pictures a child's very first day of learning.
screen: `A SLATE OF LETTERS.` → `HONEY ON EVERY ONE.` → `SAY IT, THEN TASTE IT.`

segments.voice: An old custom for a child's first day of Torah study. First, how it went. In the versions old Jewish books describe, a child was wrapped in a prayer shawl and carried to the teacher, so that even the walk felt set apart. Letters were written on a slate and covered in honey to lick off, and some versions add cakes and eggs with verses written on them, eaten after the lesson. Details vary from telling to telling. The heart doesn't: the first taste of learning is sweet. Second, the prophet who ate a scroll. In Ezekiel, the prophet is handed a scroll and told to eat it. He does, and he says: "it was in my mouth as honey for sweetness." Words, taken in so completely they become food, and they taste of honey. Third, the Psalms. Psalm nineteen calls God's teachings more precious than gold and sweeter than honey from the comb. The custom takes that line at its word: start with honey, and let the child find out the rest is sweeter still. Fourth, today. Some Jewish schools and families still put a drop of honey on a letter card when a child begins to read Hebrew. A grown-up doesn't need a slate. But the question carries: what would it take for the next thing you learn to taste sweet, not like a chore?
screen: `CARRIED TO THE TEACHER.` · `A SCROLL THAT TASTED OF HONEY.` · `SWEETER THAN THE HONEYCOMB.` · `A DROP ON A LETTER CARD.` · then, large: `LEARNING IS SWEET.`

segments.voice: If you have honey or anything sweet, put a little on your fingertip or your tongue; if you don't, imagine it. Then read one line you'd like to learn, a verse, a poem, a sentence from a book on your shelf, slowly, once, while the sweetness is still there. Close your eyes and say it back, and if it slips, read it again, letting the taste and the words arrive together.
Honey on the letters. A child's first lesson, licked off a slate, because the words were meant to taste sweet from the start. Today's word.
Your line: learning is sweet. Honey first, and then the letters, one by one. See you tomorrow.

1299.title: Coming of age
1299.hook: at thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls, one becomes responsible for the commandments
1299.howItsDone: Jews become bar or bat mitzvah by age: thirteen for boys, and twelve or thirteen for girls depending on the community. Many mark it with a synagogue ceremony and a celebration, though the status comes with the age itself.

segments.voice: Yesterday your line was learning is sweet: honey on a slate, and a child's first letters. Today, years later, that child is a teenager.

A question with a surprising answer. A Jewish boy turns thirteen. His family has no money for a party, no time to prepare, and the synagogue is closed that week for repairs. No speech. No DJ. No one even remembers it's his birthday until dinner. Is he bar mitzvah? Yes. Fully. The day he turns thirteen, by Jewish law, it has already happened. The ceremony people picture celebrates something that comes with the calendar; it doesn't create it.
screen: `NO PARTY, NO SPEECH.` → `IS HE BAR MITZVAH?` → `YES. IT ALREADY HAPPENED.`

segments.voice: Bar mitzvah. A son of the commandment; for a girl, bat mitzvah, a daughter of the commandment. First, the age. Judah ben Tema's map of a life in Pirkei Avot, the one that opened this block, has a stage that reads: at thirteen, for the commandments. For girls, the Mishnah treats twelve as the age of adulthood, and in Orthodox communities a girl becomes bat mitzvah at twelve; in some other communities, the celebration comes at thirteen, like a boy's. Second, what changes. Before this, a child is taught and encouraged, and parents carry the responsibility. After this, the young person carries it. Keeping Shabbat, fasting on Yom Kippur, counting in a prayer quorum, in communities that count them: these now belong to them. The word mitzvah means commandment; to be its son or daughter is to be the one it's addressed to. Third, the father's line. Traditionally, when a son becomes bar mitzvah, the father says a short blessing thanking God for releasing him from responsibility for this one's deeds. It can sound cold. Read another way, it's a handover, out loud: from today, your choices are yours. The blessing comes from a midrash on Jacob and Esau, twins who walked the same road until thirteen and then went their separate ways. Fourth, the party. Celebrations have grown large in some places, and they can be joyful. But as day six put it, it's not just a party. The point is a young person standing up, responsible now.
screen: `AT THIRTEEN, FOR THE COMMANDMENTS.` · `THE RESPONSIBILITY PASSES.` · `THE FATHER'S BLESSING.` · `THE PARTY IS NOT THE POINT.` · then, large: `RESPONSIBLE NOW.`

segments.voice: Think back to a moment someone handed you something for good, a key, a job, a person to care for, a decision now yours, and notice whether they said it out loud or it just happened. Then name one responsibility you carry today that's fully yours, that no one else will pick up if you don't, and hold it without judging how well you carry it. If you pray, ask for strength to carry it.
Bar mitzvah. Son of the commandment, and bat mitzvah, daughter of the commandment: the age when responsibility passes from parent to child. Today's word.
Your line: responsible now. A thirteenth birthday, and a handover said out loud. That's the day.

1300.title: Teaching at thirteen
1300.hook: the young person reads Torah and teaches the community
1300.howItsDone: At a bar or bat mitzvah, the young person is often called up to the Torah, chants the reading or the haftarah, and gives a d'var Torah, a short teaching on the week's portion, to the congregation.

segments.voice: Yesterday's word was bar mitzvah, and your line was responsible now. Today, what a young person does with that, in front of everyone.

The voice cracks on the first word. Thirteen years old, standing at the reading table, a silver pointer in one hand, the open Torah scroll in front of them, a grandmother in the third row mouthing every syllable along. The scroll has no vowels and no punctuation. They learned the melody for every word ahead of time, and now it's just them and the parchment. They get through it. Then they turn around, unfold a piece of paper, and do something even more nerve-racking. They teach. The rabbi sits down and listens.
screen: `A VOICE CRACKS ON THE FIRST WORD.` → `NO VOWELS ON THE PARCHMENT.` → `THEN THEY TEACH.`

segments.voice: First, going up. The young person is called to the Torah for an aliyah, a going up. They say the blessings before and after the reading, the same blessings any adult says, and often chant the reading itself. Some also chant a portion from the Prophets, the haftarah. In some communities girls do this too; in Orthodox communities a girl often marks her bat mitzvah with a teaching at a meal or gathering instead. Second, the teaching. It's called a d'var Torah, a word of Torah: a short talk on that week's portion. What puzzled me in it. What I think it means. Why it matters now. The child who was licking honey off letters is now explaining the text to adults. Third, the command behind it. Deuteronomy says: "and thou shalt teach them diligently unto thy children." For years, the community did exactly that. Now the line turns around, and the child teaches back: not only a receiver of the tradition, but a new link, passing it on. Fourth, who learns. The Talmud records a teacher who said he learned much from his teachers, more from his colleagues, and most of all from his students. And Pirkei Avot asks: who is wise? The one who learns from every person. When a thirteen-year-old teaches, the adults in the room get the chance to be that kind of wise.

1301.title: Akiva Learns His Letters at Forty
1301.hook: many adults celebrate a bar or bat mitzvah later in life
1301.carry: torah can be learned at any age
1301.howItsDone: Some synagogues offer adult bar and bat mitzvah classes: a group studies together and then reads from the Torah together, often including people who never had the ceremony as children.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was teach at thirteen: a young person reads the Torah, then turns around and teaches. Today, the same moment, arriving late.

Water drips onto a stone at the mouth of a well. Drip. Drip. Over years it has worn a hollow into it. A man named Akiva stands looking at it. He has never learned to read, not one letter. He's a grown man, and tradition says he's forty years old. Standing there he thinks: if soft water can carve hard stone, then surely the words of Torah, strong as iron, can carve a heart that is only flesh. He goes home, takes his young son by the hand, and the two of them sit down with the children's teacher to learn the alphabet.
screen: `WATER ON A STONE.` → `A GROWN MAN WHO CAN'T READ.` → `FATHER AND SON LEARN THE ALPHABET.`

segments.voice: First, Akiva, whom this path met with Rachel in year one. The well story is told in Avot de-Rabbi Natan, an early rabbinic collection. The man who started at forty, sitting with the children over the alphabet, became, in the tradition's memory, one of its great teachers. The rabbis didn't hide his late start. They kept it in the story. Second, Abraham. Genesis says Abraham was ninety-nine when he entered the covenant of circumcision, the covenant a baby receives at eight days old. Abraham himself came to it as an old man. Third, today. Some adults never had a bar or bat mitzvah. Their family wasn't observant, or the ceremony wasn't offered to girls where they grew up, or life simply got in the way. Now some synagogues run adult classes, where a group studies together, sometimes for a long stretch, and then stands up together to read from the Torah: a retired engineer learning the melody alongside a young nurse. Fourth, what it shows. By law, a person becomes bar or bat mitzvah with age, ceremony or not. So the adult ceremony isn't a status earned late. It's a choice made late: to stand up, to read, to teach, in front of everyone, because they want to. Water, given time, gets through stone.

1302.title: Confirmation
1302.hook: many Reform communities hold confirmation at Shavuot
1302.howItsDone: In many Reform congregations, teenagers who have continued studying after bar or bat mitzvah are confirmed as a class on Shavuot, the holiday that remembers the giving of the Torah, often speaking or leading parts of the service.

segments.voice: Yesterday's line was never too late: the grown-up standing at the Torah long after thirteen. Today, a ceremony for teenagers who have already had theirs.

A row of teenagers stands in front of the ark, a little dressed up, a little nervous. Their bar and bat mitzvahs are behind them. Since then they kept coming to a class, arguing about God, justice, and what they actually think. Now, on the holiday of Shavuot, each one stands up and speaks in front of their families and the whole congregation. In many Reform communities this is called confirmation. Why this holiday? And why a second ceremony after the one at thirteen?
screen: `TEENAGERS IN FRONT OF THE ARK.` → `ON SHAVUOT.` → `WHY HERE, AND WHY AGAIN?`

segments.voice: You met Shavuot in your first year, and Ruth's road in your second. Today they meet a class of teenagers. Jewish tradition links Shavuot to the giving of the Torah at Sinai. In Exodus, when Moses brings God's words down, the people answer together that they will do all of it. So a confirmation class stands, in a way, where that crowd stood: as a group, saying yes. A few chapters later the people say it again. In the old Jewish Publication Society translation: "All that the LORD hath spoken will we do, and obey." In Hebrew, na'aseh v'nishma: we will do, and we will hear. The Talmud tells of a heavenly voice praising Israel for promising the doing before the hearing. Some readers take it as a picture of how commitment grows: you start living it, and understanding comes along the way. Then, why again? At bar or bat mitzvah, the tradition tells a young person: you are now responsible. Confirmation lets an older teenager answer back, in their own words, about what they plan to do with that. The first yes is received. The second is chosen. And on this holiday, synagogues read the book of Ruth. Ruth isn't born into the people she joins. She chooses them, out loud, on a road: "whither thou goest, I will go." Sinai's yes and Ruth's yes sit side by side. Confirmed isn't the end of learning. It's a promise made a second time, once you know a little more of what it costs.
screen: `SHAVUOT REMEMBERS SINAI.` · `WE WILL DO, AND WE WILL HEAR.` · `THE FIRST YES, THEN THE SECOND.` · `RUTH CHOOSES ON A ROAD.` · then, large: `CONFIRMED.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind one thing you said yes to before you knew everything it would ask: a friendship, a practice, a job, a promise to yourself. Look at it as it is today, and if something in it is still worth choosing, say yes to it again, quietly, the way the class does on Shavuot. If you pray, you can carry the words from Sinai into the quiet: we will do, and we will hear.

Confirmation: a second yes, said at Shavuot. And a week closes: the firstborn redeemed, the first haircut, honey on the letters, coming of age, teaching at thirteen, never too late, and confirmed. Today's word.
Your line: confirmed. A promise can be made twice, and mean more the second time. See you tomorrow.
